https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, who was shot by ICE officers in Austin. Photograph: Wilber Rafael Garces Perez/Reuters View image in fullscreen Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, who was shot by ICE officers in Austin. Photograph: Wilber Rafael Garces Perez/Reuters Austin Venezuelan shot by ICE in Austin needs surgery to avoid losing feeling in body, supporters say Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez has bullet lodged in back as accounts differ over events leading to traffic-stop shooting Emiliano Tahui Gomez in Austin Sat 26 Sep 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 08.28 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Venezuelan man shot by federal immigration officers after a traffic stop in Texas needs surgery to avoid losing feeling on the left side of his body, according to his supporters. Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, has spent the past five days in detention with a bullet lodged in his back, after Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ) rapidly removed him from a hospital in Austin where he had been taken on Sunday after the shooting. In the days since, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the parent agency of ICE, and Garcés Pérez’s supporters have sparred over the details of events surrounding the shooting and about the quality of medical care Garcés Pérez has received while in federal immigration detention. The Democratic congressman Greg Casar, who visited Garcés Pérez on Wednesday, told reporters that he found him in a wheelchair with a sling on his left arm. Casar said Pérez only recently had been given stronger painkillers, and the injured man said he had been told by a medical specialist that he required surgery to remove the bullet stuck between his shoulder blades. “Surgery, of course, we all know, has its benefits and risks. But if Wilber and his wife decide that he needs to go through a surgery, then ICE needs to expedite his care,” Casar said. “I am making it very clear to every part of the federal government that ICE needs to take the medical care of Wilber Garcés Pérez extremely seriously.” DHS responded to Casar’s comments on X, saying it provides all its detainees comprehensive medical care that is “the best healthcare [many] have received their entire lives”. In a statement , the agency also disputed Garcés Pérez’s earlier claim that he had slept on the floor on his first night of detention. He was removed from a hospital in Austin by federal officers on the afternoon of the shooting and taken to a detention center about 140 miles away, to the west of San Antonio. DHS did not respond to questions from the Guardian regarding Garcés Pérez’s medical treatment and the investigation into the shooting that is underway. A timeline for any surgery is still unknown, Garcés Pérez’s attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said on Friday. The developments and disagreements this week have kept attention on the shooting in Austin, which rattled many in the Texas capital and state’s most liberal big city. ICE has attracted heavy criticism from some city leaders, including the mayor , Kirk Watson. Democratic politicians and migrant rights organizations have stepped up calls since the shooting for ICE to stop conducting traffic stops and random questioning of immigrants. Middle school and high school students at schools across the Austin area, including at predominantly Hispanic schools, walked out throughout the week, waving signs and flags from Latin American countries. DHS was not moved only to reiterate its position. “ICE will not be slowing down nor leaving Austin,” DHS said. A federal judge ordered that Garcés Pérez be present at a court hearing next week, where a judge is expected to begin considering a habeas corpus petition seeking his release. The local attorney general has filed a letter asking for Garcés Pérez be kept in the United States during the investigation because of his importance as a witness in his own shooting. Garcés Pérez is the subject of a court order to remove him from the US but, meanwhile, his legal team has applied for a visa on the claim that he has been the victim of violent crime by ICE. Lincoln-Goldfinch said she lost contact with her client for more than two days following a dramatic moment where he was able to get on a call with her during a press conference she was holding on Monday. He described the pain from his injuries and offered his account of events. Garcés Pérez has been kept in isolation since, she said. Meanwhile, new evidence offered by local law enforcement has called into question parts of Garcés Pérez’s account. Austin police had arrived on the scene shortly after an unnamed ICE officer had shot Garcés Pérez and he was in his car clutching his chest as federal personnel looked on, saying they had called an ambulance. Two Austin officers took a medical kit from their vehicle and were the ones to render first aid, cutting off the man’s shirt to reveal the bullet wound. Garcés Pérez, who was making a DoorDash delivery at the time he was shot, said he did not initially realize ICE was trying to stop him, and that he had driven away from federal immigration agents after an initial encounter, to move his car to a safer spot, before an ICE vehicle hit him. Bystander video showed the aftermath. Video later released by Austin police appears to show that Garcés Pérez stopped down the block from the site of the shooting about 10 minutes before it occurred. He is pulled over on a lane of moving traffic, blocked on either side by black SUVs and conversing with two federal immigration officers standing outside of his car. Austin police chief Lisa Davis said a pursuit “going through side neighborhoods” followed. Bystander video shows that an ICE SUV crashed into Garcés Pérez. A federal officer got out of the vehicle and shot him. Asked about the inconsistencies, Lincoln-Goldfinch told the Guardian: “Asking my client who is gravely injured, who is on communication lockdown, in a jail cell, to explain what happened is unfair.” She declined to say whether she regretted putting her client in front of the media on Monday. Lincoln-Goldfinch said she was also concerned about transparency because ICE has not provided her with their footage of the incident, and because of reports that the officer who shot Garcés Pérez was not wearing a body camera at the time of the shooting. DHS has said it is leading the investigation into the shooting, alongside the FBI. The local district attorney and Austin police have launched their own. https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-faces.text: BRUSSELS — The EU is facing a winter gas shortage that could leave it scrambling to replace lost energy supplies equivalent to the power used by 12 million homes, according to new reports shared with POLITICO. The shortfall raises the prospect of a winter of soaring power bills and forced energy saving measures if the bloc fails to find adequate supplies elsewhere. As the war in Iran continues to disrupt global energy supplies, the EU faces an overall shortfall this winter of up to 14 billion cubic meters of natural gas — around 7% of the bloc's demand and enough to power between 10 and 12 million European households, according to a report by the Institution for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, a U.S.-based energy think tank. Advertisement Advertisement Those conclusions are echoed in a key report by a top European body of gas network operators that was presented to national energy officials on Thursday. Natural gas is used widely to heat Europe's buildings, power its industry and generate its electricity. But the EU's gas reserves have fallen to their lowest level for the time of year since records began in 2011, at just above 70%, after high prices made it more attractive for traders to sell gas in the summer rather than store it for later use in the winter. With gas prices at near-four-year highs and supply constrained due to the U.S.-Israeli war in the Middle East, Europe has limited supply options if the coming winter proves as cold as the last, IEEFA found. While that doesn't necessarily mean the bloc will run out of gas, it does mean there could be 7 billion fewer cubic meters of stored gas to draw upon. That could force countries to buy gas at high prices on increasingly volatile global markets, or even require consumers to cut demand if fresh supplies are unavailable. The EU's record-low reserves leave the bloc "with less of a buffer" against global supply disruptions, leaving it "vulnerable to price spikes," Ana Jaller-Makarewicz, IEEFA's lead European energy analyst, said in a statement. If countries are forced to exhaust stocks this year, that would also leave them with more to refill next year, continuing the feedback loop of low reserves and higher prices, she added. The same risks were outlined in a 2026-2027 winter supply outlook published Thursday by the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas (ENTSO-G), an association of gas operators. The report warns that if imports of liquefied natural gas are limited or even “optimal” in the context of a cold winter, storage levels could fall as low as 11%, a baseline needed for strategic reserves that can't be easily tapped into. Advertisement Advertisement If countries hope to restore their reserves to 30% by the end of winter — or else face increased exposure to future cold spells — volumes equivalent to 7% of the demand will either have to be curtailed or simply withheld from consumers, ENTSO-G warns. Part of that pressure comes from a looming EU-wide ban on long-term supply contracts for Russian LNG, due to take effect in January, which will reduce European gas imports by an additional 7 billion cubic meters, according to the IEEFA report. Russian gas has been historically used to offset "swings in demand" over the winter, it said. "Now Europe depends on storage to get through winter." To make matters worse, the IEEFA report argues, gas demand over winter has crept up in the past two years, while imports to the bloc have flatlined. That's left the EU leaning harder on its reserves over the winter period, with net drawdowns rising to 22.6 billion cubic meters in January this year, up from 18.8 billion cubic meters in January 2025 and 17.8 billion cubic meters in January 2024. The alternative would be to import fresh LNG, a seaborne fuel that the EU increasingly sources from the U.S. But at current prices, importing the lost volumes would cost Europeans an additional €3 billion, a 12% rise over what the same volume would have cost last year, on top of already sky-high prices, according to the report. U.S. LNG production is also near full capacity, meaning those additional imports would further squeeze supply, Jaller-Makarewicz told POLITICO. To some, a rise in prices is more likely. While ENTSO-G's tight market scenario assumes a "global deficit" that sees available LNG imports into Europe reduced by 20%, Laurent Ruseckas, a senior gas market analyst at S&P Global Energy, argues that reserves can only ever fall so low, "since a rapid drawdown early in winter will drive up prices," drawing cargoes to Europe from Asia. "There is not much demand to destroy in Europe," he added, pointing out that the war in Ukraine already destroyed 20% of the bloc's industrial demand. "And it didn't come back." https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/13/us-t.text: One person has died and several others were injured in an incident on a roller coaster at a Six Flags park in the US state of Georgia, prompting the company to temporarily shut nine similar rides at six of its parks on Monday.A Six Flags spokesperson said the attractions, which resemble the coaster involved at Six Flags Over Georgia, were closed “out of an abundance of caution.”The park lies about 24 kilometres (15 miles) northwest of Atlanta. Officials have not said how the person died, how the others were hurt or what condition they are in. Detectives from the Cobb County Police Department’s major crimes unit are investigating.The spokesperson said the park and local authorities had responded immediately, and that Six Flags was cooperating fully with the investigation.“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” the spokesperson said, adding that the company was supporting the guests and staff affected.Neither the authorities nor Six Flags named the ride, but local television stations broadcast footage of passengers being evacuated from the Goliath coaster.According to the park’s website, Goliath opened in 2006 and reaches speeds of 70 mph (about 113 kph) and heights of 200 feet (61 metres). Over roughly three and a half minutes, riders “navigate through razor-sharp turns and soar over colossal hills,” the website says.“I cannot imagine the horror the patrons and employees witnessed today, and my heart aches for the family who lost a loved one,” said Lisa Cupid, chairwoman of the Cobb County Board of Commissioners. She said the victim’s next of kin had been informed.Cupid described the park as a major part of the county’s tourism industry, drawing visitors from across the south east of the US.“We are all grappling with how something so devastating could happen at a place that has given generations of families such happy memories,” she said.The death is at least the seventh at the Georgia park, according to the Doan Law Firm, which specialises in amusement park accidents. They include a 2006 case in which a man had a suspected heart attack on Goliath.
